newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines welcomes credit upgrade news.
newsitem.headline: Philippines welcomes credit upgrade news.

text.p: The Philippines on Friday welcomed news that its sovereign rating had been upgraded by international rating agency Standard & Poor's by one notch, bringing it closer to investment grade.

Officials and analysts said the news was expected and its immediate impact would improve the pricing of the Philippine Central Bank's maiden Yankee bond issue which is set to be launched in the second quarter. The Central Bank expects to issue bonds worth $750 million to $1.0 billion.
Standard & Poor's Corp said it had raised its rating on the Philippines' long-term foreign currency debt to BB-plus from BB.
It also upgraded the Philippines' peso-denominated debt to A-minus/A-1 from BBB-plus/A-2.
A similar upgrade is also expected soon from Moody's Investors Service Inc which announced three weeks ago that it was reviewing the Philippines for a possible upgrade.

"The Philippine Central Bank stands to immediately benefit from this development as it is set to issue its 30-year/100-year Yankee bonds very soon," Central Bank Governor Gabriel Singson said in a statement.
Analysts said the latest upgrade, however, would not have much of an impact on existing Philippine bonds in the market.

"We haven't seen too much tightening in the secondary market because the upgrade was expected. It is just one more notch up the ladder for the Philippines, which has been trading up for a year," said Carlyle Peake, vice president at Merrill Lynch in Hong Kong.
He noted that many Philippine bonds already are trading like investment grade credits.
Many analysts expect the Philippines to be upgraded to investment grade in the near future.
Some said it could come after May next year once the presidential elections are held.

"Investment grade rating will not be that far away. The earliest will be after the elections when the market has confirmed the qualified successor to President Ramos," said Noel Reyes, a trader of ING Bank in Manila.
But others thought it may come sooner.
"When we exit from the International Monetary Fund come June, we would have better chances to investment grade sooner than we expect," said Helen Alvarez, research head of All Asia Securities.

"The Philippine government is determined more than ever to complete its economic reform programme, permanently graduate from IMF conditional borrowing by June this year, and finally achieve investment-grade rating on its sovereign foreign currency debt," said Governor Singson in his statement.

The Philippines is optimistic that it can exit from 34 years of IMF supervision this year when it expedites the passage into law of the remaining portion of its comprehensive tax reform package that will provide a solid revenue base for the government. -- Manila newsroom (632) 841-8937
